passage: I'm Sabina. In Class 6 I made a joke about Bhupen's old school bag, and half the class hooted. It felt like being lit up from inside. So I made another joke the next day, and another. But the cheering was thin. The moment I stopped, the same faces turned to their notebooks, and nobody asked me to sit with them at lunch. Bhupen never looked up at me at all; he ate alone by the window. That afternoon I understood that those claps had never meant respect. I stopped the jokes, and at lunch I offered him half my orange. He looked surprised and said thanks, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Sabina make a joke about?
qa.a: Sabina made a joke about Bhupen's old school bag.

qa.q: Why did Sabina stop making jokes about Bhupen?
qa.a: Sabina saw that the cheering was thin and faded once the jokes stopped, and understood it had never meant real respect.

qa.q: What did Sabina do after stopping the jokes, and why might it matter to Bhupen?
qa.a: Sabina offered him half an orange at lunch, a small kind step that showed him respect after the mockery.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt eating alone by the window while the class cheered the jokes?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and lonely, since he never looked up at Sabina and ate by himself.

grounding: A child mocks a classmate for the applause, sees the cheering is empty, and chooses respect.

passage: I'm Siddharth. During the free period I saw two big boys shoving a small Class 5 boy called Tarun back and forth in the corridor. Most of us looked at our shoes. Manoj did not. His face crumpled, as if it hurt him too. He did not shout. Afterwards he sat next to Tarun on the steps and offered him a biscuit. Then he said quietly, "Let's tell Sir," and I said I would come along. I think Manoj was scared, but he did it anyway. He told me later that he did not feel like a hero, only tired of watching.

qa.q: What did Manoj offer Tarun after sitting next to him?
qa.a: He offered him a biscuit.

qa.q: What does Manoj's crumpled face suggest he felt when he saw Tarun being shoved?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sorry for Tarun and was upset by it, though Siddharth also thinks Manoj was scared.

qa.q: What small actions helped Tarun without anyone fighting?
qa.a: Manoj sat with Tarun, shared a biscuit and suggested telling Sir, and Siddharth joined him.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Manoj sat next to him?
qa.a: Tarun was probably comforted to see someone care after so many people looked away.

grounding: A child feels sorry for a boy being pushed around and helps with small acts, not heroics.

passage: Monday: On the school bus, two older girls took Bidisha's hair clips and tossed them over her head. Nazia's mouth went dry. If she spoke, she thought, they would start on her next. She said nothing and watched the traffic. Wednesday: She wrote a short note without her name and dropped it into the teacher's box. Her hand shook. Friday: At the bus stop, Nazia sat down next to Bidisha and offered her a peppermint. "Those girls were awful," she said softly. Bidisha nodded. The teacher had begun sitting on the bus each morning, and nobody asked who had written the note.

qa.q: How did Nazia let the teacher know without giving her name?
qa.a: She wrote a short note without her name and dropped it into the teacher's box.

qa.q: Why did Nazia stay silent on Monday?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she spoke up, the older girls would start on her next.

qa.q: What safe choices did Nazia find when she was too scared to confront the girls?
qa.a: She reported it anonymously with a note, and then she was kind to Bidisha afterwards.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Nazia sat beside her and offered a peppermint?
qa.a: Bidisha probably felt comforted and less alone, since someone had noticed and spoke kindly, and she nodded in agreement.

grounding: A frightened bystander reports quietly and is kind to the target afterwards, over several days.

passage: Kunal kept replaying it at bedtime: Samir pressed against the compound wall in the colony park while two boys snatched his kite spool, and Kunal standing there with his cycle, not moving. The tightness under his ribs would not go away. Next morning he walked to Samir's building and knocked. "I saw what happened yesterday," he said. "I should have come over. Are you okay?" Samir shrugged, but he let Kunal in. After a while Kunal asked, "Can we tell your mother, or my Papa?" and Samir, after a long moment, nodded. The bad feeling did not vanish, but now it had somewhere to go.

qa.q: Where was Samir when the two boys snatched his kite spool?
qa.a: He was pressed against the compound wall in the colony park.

qa.q: Why did the tightness under Kunal's ribs stay with him at bedtime?
qa.a: He felt guilty that he had watched and done nothing to help Samir.

qa.q: What did Kunal do that turned his guilt into something useful?
qa.a: He visited Samir, admitted he should have come over, asked if he was okay, and suggested telling an adult.

qa.q: How might Samir see Kunal's visit after being left alone in the park?
qa.a: Samir shrugged at first but let him in and later nodded, so he probably felt cautious yet glad that someone cared.

grounding: A child who watched and did nothing feels guilty and acts by checking in and involving an adult.

passage: In the hostel dining hall, someone started a rhyme about Hansa's two long plaits, and the whole table cracked up. Santosh laughed with them, though his laugh came out too loud. Then he saw Hansa's tray trembling and her eyes fixed on her plate, and the laugh stuck in his throat. He knew why he had joined in: he could not bear being the one left alone at the end of the bench. The next evening, when the same boy began the rhyme again, Santosh looked at his rice and did not laugh. Then he picked up his tray and sat down across from Hansa. "Hi," he said. It was small, and a little scary, but the rhyme fizzled out.

qa.q: Where did the rhyme about Hansa's plaits take place?
qa.a: It took place in the hostel dining hall.

qa.q: Why did Santosh laugh at the rhyme about Hansa?
qa.a: He did not want to be left out or end up alone at the end of the bench, so he went along with everyone else.

qa.q: What small refusals did Santosh make the next evening, and what effect did they have?
qa.a: He did not laugh and he moved to sit across from Hansa, and the rhyme fizzled out without an audience.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh sat across from her?
qa.a: She may have felt some relief at a bit of kindness after the laughter, though the passage does not say how she reacted.

grounding: A child laughs because everyone does, sees the target's hurt, and next time refuses and moves to sit with her.

passage: Tuesday. Today Maya and her friends laughed at my new haircut in the corridor. I went and sat on the bench by the library and pretended to read. Then Rafiq came over and sat next to me. He did not say much. He just asked, "Are you okay?" and stayed there until the bell rang. That tiny thing made my throat go tight, but in a good way. I said thanks, and he shrugged like it was nothing. It was not nothing to me. I felt less alone than I have all week. Maybe one day I will sit next to somebody like that too. -- Jahnavi

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi sit after the laughing?
qa.a: Jahnavi sat on the bench by the library.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi's throat go tight in a good way when Rafiq sat alongside?
qa.a: Jahnavi was touched by his kindness and felt less alone.

qa.q: How could Jahnavi pass this kindness on later?
qa.a: Jahnavi could sit beside someone who has been teased and quietly ask if they are okay.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see his own small act?
qa.a: He shrugged as though it was nothing, so he may not realise how much it meant to Jahnavi; he probably just wanted to make sure Jahnavi was okay.

grounding: A teased child records how one classmate's quiet company eased that loneliness.

passage: I'm Jasleen. At recess I saw three boys empty a smaller boy's pencil box into the dustbin, and I could not stop thinking about it all through Hindi class. I was scared people would call me a snitch. After the bell I waited until the room was empty and went to Rajni Ma'am's desk. "Ma'am, can I tell you something? Please don't say it was me." She listened and nodded. She said she would deal with it in a way that did not point to me. I walked home relieved but a little shaky. Later I decided that speaking up to keep someone safe is a different thing from tattling.

qa.q: What did the three boys do to the smaller boy's pencil box?
qa.a: They emptied it into the dustbin at recess.

qa.q: What was Jasleen worried about before she went to the teacher?
qa.a: Jasleen was afraid other students would find out and call Jasleen a snitch.

qa.q: How can a teacher make it safer for a child like Jasleen to speak up?
qa.a: The teacher can listen, keep the child's name private and deal with it without pointing at the child, as Rajni Ma'am promised.

qa.q: How might the smaller boy be affected by Jasleen speaking up?
qa.a: He may be protected without having to report it himself, since the teacher can step in to stop the three boys.

grounding: A bystander quietly tells the teacher what was seen, worrying about being called a snitch.

passage: I'm Aditi. During art period my friend Ishan nudged me and whispered, "Look at Yash's drawing, it's a potato. Say something, everyone's going to." A few girls were already giggling. I felt torn: I wanted Ishan to like me, but I also knew Yash was trying hard. My mouth stayed shut for a moment. Then I said, quiet but clear, "I don't want to," and took my pencil box to the front table. Ishan rolled his eyes. That evening he texted me: "sorry, that was mean of me". I had not expected that. Maybe saying no can make a friend think.

qa.q: What did Ishan say Yash's drawing looked like?
qa.a: He said it was a potato.

qa.q: Why did Aditi feel torn when Ishan nudged?
qa.a: Aditi wanted Ishan to like Aditi but also knew Yash was trying hard, so Aditi was pulled between fitting in and doing right.

qa.q: What could Aditi say if a friend pushes again to mock someone?
qa.a: Aditi can repeat "I don't want to" and walk away, as before, because real friends respect that.

qa.q: How might Ishan see Aditi's refusal afterwards?
qa.a: Ishan first rolled his eyes, but that evening he admitted it was mean, so the refusal seems to have made him think.

grounding: A child pressured by a friend to mock a classmate says no and walks away, and the friend reconsiders.

passage: Class teacher's note. Yesterday in the corridor I watched Seema walk past while two boys blocked Jomon's way and took his cap. She did not look at him and kept her eyes on her water bottle. When I asked her about it later, she shrugged and said, "Not my problem." I said I was not scolding, only asking. She was quiet for a while and then said that everybody else had walked by too. I asked if she would like to help next time, and she said she would think about it. I have spoken with Jomon and the two boys. I will check in with Seema on Friday and ask her and Jomon to help me set up the library shelves.

qa.q: What did Seema say when the teacher asked her about it?
qa.a: She shrugged and said, "Not my problem."

qa.q: What does Seema's staring at her water bottle suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uncomfortable and wanted to avoid getting involved, telling herself it was not her problem, though the teacher cannot be certain.

qa.q: What could Seema do next time she sees a child being blocked and taunted?
qa.a: She could tell an adult, stay near the child or ask if they are okay, so nobody is left alone just because everyone assumes someone else will help.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt as people walked past?
qa.a: Jomon was probably lonely and hurt as people walked by without helping.

grounding: A teacher's note about a child who tells herself it is not her problem and turns away from someone being bullied.

passage: Saturday night. They are shouting again downstairs. My heart is going so fast I can hear it in my ears. I am sitting on my bed with a pillow on my knees. I keep thinking something is breaking, like our whole family could crack. I know being scared is allowed. So I did what I practised: breathed in slowly, breathed out, and went to sit on the balcony with my torch and my comic. The shouting sounds smaller from there. Tomorrow I will tell Chacha Pankaj how it feels. He always listens without fixing everything at once. -- Hrithik

qa.q: Where did Hrithik go to sit with the comic?
qa.a: Hrithik went to sit on the balcony with a torch and the comic.

qa.q: What was Hrithik afraid of on hearing the shouting?
qa.a: Hrithik feared something was breaking, like the whole family cracking, and the racing heart shows how frightened Hrithik was.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do to calm down, and what comes next?
qa.a: Hrithik breathed slowly and moved to the balcony, and plans to tell Chacha Pankaj how it feels.

qa.q: How might Chacha Pankaj see Hrithik coming to talk?
qa.a: He may be glad that Hrithik trusts him, since Hrithik says he always listens, and he may want to make sure Hrithik feels safe.

grounding: A child frightened by parents' shouting calms down, goes to a safe place and plans to talk to a trusted adult.
